name: Natural numbers
definition: The counting numbers 1, 2, 3, … (some authors include 0; check the local convention). They support induction: prove a base case and the step from n to n+1.

examples.explanation: n is a natural number.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Integers
definition: All whole numbers, positive, negative and zero: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …. The symbol comes from German “Zahlen” (numbers).

examples.explanation: Negative three is an integer.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Rational numbers
definition: All ratios of integers with nonzero denominator. Decimals of rationals always terminate or repeat; anything else is irrational.

examples.explanation: Two thirds is rational.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Real numbers
definition: All rationals plus irrationals: every point on the number line. The reals are complete, meaning limits of convergent sequences stay inside.

examples.explanation: Root two is real but not rational.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Complex numbers
definition: Numbers a + bi with real a, b and i² = −1. Every nonzero complex number has a magnitude and an angle; every polynomial equation has a complex root (fundamental theorem of algebra).

examples.explanation: Real part 3, imaginary part 4.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Imaginary unit
definition: The number with i² = −1, extending the reals to the complex plane. Engineers often write j instead, since i means current.

examples.explanation: Powers of i cycle every four.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Complex conjugate
definition: Reflects a complex number across the real axis by negating its imaginary part. A number times its conjugate gives its squared magnitude.

examples.explanation: Flip the sign of the imaginary part.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Real and imaginary parts
definition: Extract the components of z = a + bi: Re(z) = a and Im(z) = b. Note Im(z) is the real number b, not bi.
reading: “the real part of z” and “the imaginary part of z”.

examples.explanation: Components of 3 + 4i.

commonMistakes: Writing Im(3+4i) = 4i; the imaginary part is the real coefficient 4.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Complex modulus
definition: The distance of z from the origin: |a + bi| = √(a² + b²). It generalizes absolute value to the complex plane and equals √(z·z̄).

examples.explanation: A 3-4-5 triangle from the origin.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Euler's identity
definition: Links five fundamental constants in one equation. It is the special case x = π of Euler's formula e^(ix) = cos x + i·sin x.
reading: “e to the i pi plus one equals zero”.

examples.explanation: Euler's formula: rotation in the complex plane.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 4
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Gamma function
definition: Extends the factorial to non-integers: Γ(n) = (n−1)! for positive integers, defined by an integral elsewhere. It appears in probability distributions and volume formulas.

examples.explanation: At integers it recovers the factorial, shifted by one.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 5
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Beta function
definition: A two-argument special function closely tied to gamma: B(x,y) = Γ(x)Γ(y)/Γ(x+y). It normalizes the beta distribution in probability.

examples.explanation: Beta expressed through gamma.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 5
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Riemann zeta function
definition: Sums 1/nˢ over all positive integers. Its values at even integers involve powers of π; its zeros encode the distribution of primes, including the unproven Riemann hypothesis.

examples.explanation: The Basel problem: reciprocals of squares sum to π²/6.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 25
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Error function
definition: Captures areas under the bell curve: erf(x) is twice the normal area from 0 to x. Normal probabilities are arithmetic with erf.

examples.explanation: Scaled area under the Gaussian bell.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 7
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Bessel function
definition: Oscillating special functions solving radial wave problems: vibrations of drums, heat in cylinders, signal modes. J_n is the Bessel function of the first kind of order n.

examples.explanation: The zero-order Bessel function starts at 1 like cosine.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 10
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Group
definition: A set G with one operation satisfying closure, associativity, an identity element and inverses. Groups capture symmetry: rotations, permutations and number systems all form groups.

examples.explanation: Integers under addition: identity 0, inverse −n.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Isomorphism
definition: A structure-preserving correspondence between two objects: a bijection carrying the operations across. Isomorphic objects are algebraically the same, differing only in labels.

examples.explanation: The exponential maps addition to multiplication bijectively.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

notes: Shares the ≅ glyph with geometric congruence; the algebraic reading is set by context.

name: Modular congruence
definition: States that a and b leave the same remainder on division by n, equivalently n divides their difference. Congruence classes partition the integers into n residue systems.
reading: “a is congruent to b mod n”.

examples.explanation: Both leave remainder 5; their difference 12 is a multiple of 12.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 27
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Greatest common divisor
definition: The largest integer dividing both a and b. Euclid's algorithm computes it with repeated remainders; it underlies fraction reduction and modular inverses.
reading: “the g c d of a and b”.

examples.explanation: Six is the largest shared divisor.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Least common multiple
definition: The smallest positive integer that is a multiple of both a and b. It gives the least common denominator for adding fractions, and satisfies gcd(a,b)·lcm(a,b) = a·b.
reading: “the l c m of a and b”.

examples.explanation: Twelve is the first shared multiple.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Euler's totient function
definition: Counts integers from 1 to n that share no factor with n. It powers RSA cryptography via Euler's theorem: a^φ(n) ≡ 1 mod n for a coprime to n.

examples.explanation: 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 are coprime to 9.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 27
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Tensor product
definition: Builds a larger vector space from two smaller ones, with dimension multiplied. It combines quantum states, extends scalars, and writes the Kronecker product of matrices.

examples.explanation: Dimensions multiply under the tensor product.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

sources.label: Unicode Mathematical Operators code chart
sources.license: Unicode License Agreement; glyph identity

name: Direct sum (exclusive or)
definition: In algebra, the direct sum combines structures component-wise. In logic and computing, the same glyph means exclusive or: exactly one side true.

examples.explanation: Dimensions add under direct sum.
Exactly one of P, Q holds.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

sources.label: Unicode Mathematical Operators code chart
sources.license: Unicode License Agreement; glyph identity

name: Arg min and arg max
definition: Name where a minimum or maximum occurs, rather than its value. argmin f is the input achieving the smallest output; argmax the largest.

examples.explanation: The square is smallest at x = 3.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Fourier transform
definition: Decomposes a signal into its frequencies: the transform at each frequency measures how much of that oscillation the signal contains. It turns differentiation into multiplication and convolution into products.

examples.explanation: Correlate f against every oscillation frequency.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Laplace transform
definition: Converts differential equations into algebra by mapping functions of time to functions of a complex frequency s. Derivatives become multiplication by s, so circuits and controls solve with fractions.

examples.explanation: Differentiation becomes multiplication by s.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Big-O notation
definition: Bounds growth from above up to a constant factor: f is O(g) when |f| ≤ C·g eventually. It classifies algorithms (linear, quadratic, exponential) while ignoring hardware constants.

examples.explanation: Quadratic term dominates; constants and lower terms drop.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

notes: Uses the Latin letter O, not omicron, by convention.

name: Big-Theta notation
definition: Bounds growth tightly from both sides: f is Θ(g) when squeezed between constant multiples of g eventually. It states the true order of growth, unlike the one-sided O or Ω.

examples.explanation: Sandwiched between 3n² and 4n² for large n: bounded above and below.

sources.label: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures, Theta
sources.license: NIST DADS (U.S. federal reference); consulted, original wording

name: Big-Omega notation
definition: Bounds growth from below: f is Ω(g) when it stays above some constant multiple of g from some point on. The DADS definition requires this for all large n, which is stronger than some textbooks' infinitely-often version.

examples.explanation: n² stays above 1·n from n = 1 onward.

sources.label: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures, Omega
sources.license: NIST DADS (U.S. federal reference); consulted, original wording

name: Euler–Mascheroni constant
definition: The limiting gap between harmonic growth and the logarithm: γ = lim(Hₙ − ln n) ≈ 0.57721, where Hₙ = 1 + 1/2 + … + 1/n. It appears in series evaluations, zeta values and number theory.

examples.explanation: Harmonic sums outrun the logarithm by this constant amount.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 5
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Prime-counting function
definition: Counts the primes up to x: π(x) = Σ_{p≤x} 1. The prime number theorem says π(x) ~ x/ln x: primes thin out logarithmically, with the ratio tending to 1.

examples.explanation: The primes 2, 3, 5 and 7 do not exceed 10.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 27
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Möbius function
definition: Encodes square factors: μ(n) = (−1)ᵏ for a product of k distinct primes, 0 when any square divides n, and μ(1) = 1. It inverts sums over divisors (Möbius inversion).

examples.explanation: 30 = 2·3·5 has three distinct prime factors: (−1)³.
12 = 2²·3 has the squared divisor 4.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 27
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Prime number
definition: An integer above 1 divisible only by 1 and itself. Every integer above 1 factors uniquely into primes (the fundamental theorem of arithmetic), and there are infinitely many of them.

examples.explanation: Twelve's unique prime factorization: two squared times three.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 27
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Holomorphic function
definition: A complex function differentiable at every point of an open set, far stronger than real differentiability. Holomorphic functions are automatically infinitely differentiable and equal their Taylor series; entire means holomorphic everywhere.

examples.explanation: Differentiable at every complex point, hence holomorphic on the whole plane.

contexts.meaning: Holomorphic and analytic coincide for complex functions (unlike smooth-but-not-analytic real cases).

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

notes: Standard first-course complex-analysis definition; cross-checked against the Cauchy framing used across references.

name: Topological space
definition: A set X with a collection T of subsets called open sets, satisfying: ∅ and X are open, arbitrary unions of opens are open, finite intersections are open. This generalizes distance-based geometry to spaces with no metric.

examples.explanation: A valid topology on X = {a, b}: unions and finite intersections stay inside.

sources.label: LibreTexts, Introduction to Topological Spaces
sources.license: Public Domain (page footer); consulted, original wording

name: Compactness
definition: Every open cover has a finite subcover: the set is, in a precise sense, finitely large. In ℝⁿ this is exactly closed and bounded (Heine–Borel); continuous images of compact sets stay compact, so extrema are attained.

examples.explanation: The closed interval qualifies; the open one fails closedness (and its cover by (1/n, 1) has no finite subcover).

sources.label: LibreTexts, Introduction to Topological Spaces
sources.license: Public Domain (page footer); consulted, original wording

notes: Heine–Borel and finite-subcover formulations cross-checked against UChicago May REU topology notes excerpts.

name: Connectedness
definition: A space that cannot be split into two disjoint nonempty open pieces: it is all one piece. Path-connected (joinable by paths) implies connected; intervals are the connected subsets of ℝ.

examples.explanation: Two separated open parts witness the split; neither piece alone disconnects.

sources.label: LibreTexts, Introduction to Topological Spaces
sources.license: Public Domain (page footer); consulted, original wording

notes: Separation-based definition cross-checked against UChicago May REU topology notes excerpts.

name: Homeomorphism
definition: A continuous bijection with continuous inverse: the two spaces are topologically the same, differing only by stretching. Properties surviving homeomorphism (compactness, connectedness) are the topological invariants.

examples.explanation: x ↦ tan(π(x − 1/2)) stretches the bounded interval onto the whole line, reversibly.

sources.label: LibreTexts, Introduction to Topological Spaces
sources.license: Public Domain (page footer); consulted, original wording

notes: Continuous-bijection-with-continuous-inverse formulation cross-checked against UChicago May REU topology notes excerpts. Shares ≅ with geometric congruence and algebraic isomorphism; context decides.

name: Manifold
definition: A space that locally looks like ordinary Euclidean space: every point has a neighborhood resembling an open piece of ℝⁿ. Curves, surfaces, and spacetime models are 1-, 2- and 4-manifolds.

examples.explanation: The circle: removing any point leaves something shaped like an open interval, so it is locally one-dimensional.

sources.label: LibreTexts, Introduction to Topological Spaces
sources.license: Public Domain (page footer); consulted, original wording

name: Ring
definition: A set with addition (an abelian group) and a compatible multiplication: associative, distributive over addition. Commutative rings, like the integers, also commute multiplicatively.

examples.explanation: The integers: addition and multiplication satisfy every ring axiom.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Field
definition: A commutative ring where every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse: division (except by zero) always works. Rationals, reals and complex numbers are fields; integers are not.

examples.explanation: The rationals form a field; 2 has no integer inverse, so ℤ does not.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Homomorphism
definition: A map between same-type structures that preserves the operations: the image of a product is the product of the images. Its kernel (elements sent to the identity) measures how far it is from an isomorphism.

examples.explanation: Parity mod 2: adding integers then reducing matches reducing then adding.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Diophantine equation
definition: A polynomial equation whose solutions are sought in integers (or rationals). Some have infinitely many solutions, some none, deciding which drove centuries of number theory, including Fermat's Last Theorem.

examples.explanation: The smallest Pythagorean triple: (3, 4, 5) solves x² + y² = z² in integers.

sources.label: MacTutor, Fermat's last theorem
sources.license: © University of St Andrews (MacTutor); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Shannon entropy
definition: Measures uncertainty in bits: H = −Σ p·log₂ p over the outcomes. A fair coin has entropy 1 (one yes/no question resolves it); certain outcomes carry zero entropy.

examples.explanation: A fair coin flip holds exactly one bit of uncertainty.

sources.label: Scholarpedia, Entropy (Downarowicz)
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 (page footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Turing machine
definition: An abstract computer: finitely many states plus an infinite tape, stepping by a transition function δ from (state, symbol) to (symbol, move, state). The model defines computability itself via the Church–Turing thesis; the halting problem shows its limits.

examples.explanation: The transition function: in state q reading s, what to write, where to move, and what state comes next.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Turing Machines
sources.license: SEP (open access); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Fundamental theorem of algebra
definition: Every non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients has a complex root, hence exactly n roots counting multiplicity for degree n. The complex numbers are algebraically closed: no extension is ever needed.

examples.explanation: Degree two, two complex roots: the reals alone could not factor it.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Fermat's Last Theorem
definition: xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ has no nonzero integer solutions for n > 2. Conjectured by Fermat around 1637 and proved by Wiles (with Taylor) in 1995 via elliptic curves and modularity.

examples.explanation: No nonzero integers satisfy even the n = 4 case, which Fermat himself proved.

sources.label: MacTutor, Fermat's last theorem
sources.license: © University of St Andrews (MacTutor); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Riemann hypothesis
definition: All nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function lie on the critical line Re(s) = 1/2. Unproven since 1859, it would pin down the fine distribution of primes; verified computationally for the first trillions of zeros.

examples.explanation: The first zero up the critical line, at height about t = 14.13.

commonMistakes: Calling it proven; extensive computation is evidence, not proof.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 25
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

notes: Zero locations cross-checked against the published zero tables referenced across analytic number theory literature.

name: Sigma-algebra
definition: A collection M of subsets of a set X containing X itself and closed under complements and countable unions (hence also countable intersections). Its members are the measurable sets: exactly those a measure is allowed to size.

examples.explanation: The power set of {1, 2}: the largest sigma-algebra on two points.

commonMistakes: Settling for closure under finite unions: that gives an algebra of sets, not a sigma-algebra, and measures need the countable case for limits.

sources.label: PlanetMath, σ-algebra
sources.license: CC BY-SA (PlanetMath); consulted, original wording, no text reused

name: Hilbert space
definition: A vector space with an inner product in which every Cauchy sequence converges to a point inside: complete in the induced norm ‖x‖ = √⟨x,x⟩. Finite-dimensional inner-product spaces qualify automatically; square-integrable functions are the canonical infinite-dimensional example.

examples.explanation: With the dot product: every Cauchy sequence of vectors converges, so completeness is automatic in finite dimensions.

sources.label: LibreTexts, Function Spaces (Fowler, UVA)
sources.license: Page license not declared; consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

notes: Completeness formulation cross-checked against UBC metric-completeness notes and a CalPoly Hilbert-space thesis (search excerpts); the entry follows the opened Fowler text.

name: Category
definition: Objects together with morphisms between them, equipped with associative composition and an identity morphism per object. Groups, spaces, and vector spaces each form categories with their structure-preserving maps.

examples.explanation: Groups as objects, group homomorphisms as morphisms, composed as functions.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Category Theory
sources.license: SEP (open access); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Morphism
definition: An arrow f: X → Y with a domain and codomain. Morphisms compose when target meets source, associatively, with identities doing nothing. An isomorphism has a two-sided inverse; mono and epi generalize injective and surjective.

examples.explanation: With f: X → Y and g: Y → Z, the composite runs X through both steps.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Category Theory
sources.license: SEP (open access); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Functor
definition: A structure-preserving map between categories: objects to objects, morphisms to morphisms, respecting composition and identities. Covariant functors keep arrow direction; contravariant ones reverse it.

examples.explanation: The forgetful functor keeps each group's underlying set and sends homomorphisms to plain functions.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Category Theory
sources.license: SEP (open access); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Natural transformation
definition: A coherent family of morphisms η_X: F(X) → G(X), one per object, making every naturality square commute: G(f)∘η_X = η_Y∘F(f). When each component is an isomorphism, the functors are naturally isomorphic.

examples.explanation: Each set embeds in its power set; maps commute with the embedding, uniformly in X.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Category Theory
sources.license: SEP (open access); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Equivalence of categories
definition: Functors F, G in opposite directions with natural isomorphisms GF ≅ Id and FG ≅ Id: the categories have the same structure up to isomorphism. This is strictly weaker than isomorphism of categories (rare on-the-nose equality) and it is the notion that matters in practice.

examples.explanation: Groups carry strictly more structure than sets (e.g. Grp has a zero object, Set does not), yet functors still relate them.

commonMistakes: Demanding an isomorphism of categories (bijection on objects); equivalence only asks essential surjectivity plus fully faithfulness.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Category Theory
sources.license: SEP (open access); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Universal property
definition: Characterizes an object by unique morphisms to or from it, not by internal structure: initial objects receive none-but (maps out uniquely), terminal objects receive exactly one map from each object, and a zero object is both. Products, limits, and free constructions are all universal in this sense.

examples.explanation: Every set has exactly one map into a singleton: the universal property of a one-point set.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Category Theory
sources.license: SEP (open access); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Limit and colimit
definition: Universal cones over (limit) and under (colimit) a diagram. Products, pullbacks, equalizers, and terminal objects are limits; coproducts, pushouts, coequalizers, and initial objects are colimits. Left adjoints preserve colimits, right adjoints preserve limits.

examples.explanation: The product with its two projections: any pair of maps into A and B factors uniquely through it.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Category Theory
sources.license: SEP (open access); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Adjoint functors
definition: Functors F: C → D and G: D → C in opposite directions with unit η: Id → GF and counit ε: FG → Id satisfying the triangle identities. F is the optimal way to build D-structure from C-data (free groups from sets); G forgets back.

examples.explanation: Free groups are left adjoint to forgetting group structure: the universal way to put generators into a group.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Category Theory
sources.license: SEP (open access); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Linear operator
definition: An additive, homogeneous map between vector spaces: T(ax + y) = aT(x) + T(y). Every operator has a domain, codomain, range, and kernel; finite-dimensional ones are exactly matrices.

examples.explanation: Linearity checks out: scaling and adding inputs scales and adds outputs.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Self-adjoint operator
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Operator norm
definition: The largest stretch factor: ‖T‖ = sup ‖Tx‖ over unit vectors. Finite exactly for bounded operators; submultiplicative (‖ST‖ ≤ ‖S‖‖T‖), so bounded operators form an algebra.

examples.explanation: The identity stretches nothing: every unit vector stays unit.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Self-adjoint operator
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Bounded and unbounded operators
definition: Bounded operators send bounded sets to bounded sets, equivalently, for linear maps, they are continuous, with finite operator norm. Unbounded operators (like differentiation) can only be densely defined; an everywhere-defined symmetric operator is automatically bounded.

examples.explanation: In finite dimensions every linear map is continuous: unboundedness is an infinite-dimensional phenomenon.

commonMistakes: Assuming differentiation-style operators can live everywhere; unbounded operators always come with a restricted domain.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Self-adjoint operator
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Adjoint operator
definition: The operator T* defined by ⟨Tx, y⟩ = ⟨x, T*y⟩. In finite dimensions it is the conjugate transpose; for unbounded operators it lives on the subspace where the relation makes sense, which is why domains matter.

examples.explanation: Transpose and conjugate each entry.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Self-adjoint operator
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Self-adjoint operator
definition: Densely defined with A = A*, including equal domains. Symmetric (⟨Ax,y⟩ = ⟨x,Ay⟩ on its domain) is strictly weaker: a symmetric operator can fail to be self-adjoint when its adjoint lives on a larger domain. Observables in quantum mechanics must be self-adjoint, with real spectrum.

examples.explanation: Diagonal and real: equals its own conjugate transpose.

commonMistakes: Calling symmetric enough; without domain equality the spectral guarantees fail.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Self-adjoint operator
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Normal and unitary operators
definition: Normal operators commute with their adjoint (N*N = NN*): self-adjoint and unitary operators are the key cases, all unitarily diagonalizable in finite dimensions. Unitary operators (U*U = I) preserve lengths; their eigenvalues sit on the unit circle.

examples.explanation: Quarter-turn rotation: unitary, with eigenvalues ±i on the unit circle.

contexts.meaning: Commutes with its adjoint; unitarily diagonalizable.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Spectral theorem
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Projection operator
definition: Idempotent operators (P² = P): applying twice changes nothing after the first. Orthogonal projections add P* = P and split the space into range plus orthogonal kernel; spectral measures assemble operators from them.

examples.explanation: Projecting twice onto the x-axis lands where the first projection put you.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Spectral theorem
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Compact operator
definition: Maps bounded sets to sets with compact closure, norm-limits of finite-rank operators on Hilbert space. The spectrum is discrete except possibly 0, and compact self-adjoint operators keep an orthonormal eigenbasis: the friendliest infinite-dimensional case.

examples.explanation: Eigenvalues 1/n accumulate only at 0: the signature of compactness.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Spectral theorem
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Spectrum and resolvent
definition: The λ for which A − λI fails to be invertible. Eigenvalues (point spectrum) are only part of it: continuous and residual spectrum appear in infinite dimensions. The complement is the resolvent set; self-adjoint spectra are real.

examples.explanation: Multiplication by t on L²[0,1] has this whole interval as spectrum, with no eigenvalues at all.

commonMistakes: Equating spectrum with eigenvalues; the distinction only collapses in finite dimensions.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Spectral theorem
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Spectral theorem
definition: Self-adjoint (and more generally normal) operators diagonalize in an orthonormal basis in finite dimensions. Infinite dimensions need care: compact self-adjoint keeps eigenvectors; general bounded self-adjoint becomes multiplication operators or projection-valued integrals.

examples.explanation: Symmetric with eigenvalues 3 and 1 along (1,1) and (1,−1): diagonalizable by rotation.

name: Chain complex
definition: Modules (or abelian groups) linked by differentials with d² = 0: the image of each map lands in the kernel of the next. Cochain complexes run the arrows upward; everything else carries over with degrees reversed.

examples.explanation: Multiplication by 2 with zeros around it: consecutive composites vanish trivially.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Chain complex
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Homology
definition: Cycles modulo boundaries: Hₙ = ker(dₙ)/im(dₙ₊₁). It measures exactly how far a complex is from exactness, zero homology means every cycle is a boundary. H₀ counts path components.

examples.explanation: For a path-connected space: one component, one copy of ℤ.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Chain complex
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Cohomology
definition: Homology of a cochain complex: same ker/im construction with arrows running upward. De Rham cohomology reads closed differential forms modulo exact ones, detecting holes analytically rather than combinatorially.

examples.explanation: The circle's loop integral detects one independent hole.

commonMistakes: Treating cohomology as just homology with raised indices; the contravariant behavior and ring structure genuinely differ.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Chain complex
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Chain map
definition: Degree-wise maps between complexes commuting with the differentials: d∘f = f∘d at every level. Chain maps send cycles to cycles and boundaries to boundaries, hence induce maps on homology.

examples.explanation: A continuous map of spaces induces maps on homology groups.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Chain complex
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Exact sequence
definition: A complex with zero homology everywhere: image equals kernel at each spot. Short exact (0 → A → B → C → 0) means injective start and surjective end; a short exact sequence of complexes unrolls into a long exact sequence in homology.

examples.explanation: Multiply by m is injective; its cokernel is the integers mod m.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Chain complex
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Cokernel
definition: The codomain modulo the image: what the map fails to hit. Dual to the kernel (which measures failure of injectivity); together they bookend every homomorphism.

examples.explanation: Doubling misses exactly the odd integers.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Chain complex
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Projective resolutions
definition: An exact sequence of projective modules onto M: a 'best approximation' by well-behaved pieces, used to compute derived functors. Free modules are projective; injective modules dualize the picture (divisible groups over ℤ).

examples.explanation: A free (hence projective) resolution of ℤ/m: exact except at the end, where homology reads the module back.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Chain complex
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

notes: Projective/injective machinery cross-checked against UT Austin homological-algebra lecture-note excerpts (Lecture 4).

name: Derived functor
aliases: long exact sequence of derived functors
definition: Extends a half-exact functor to a long exact sequence: left-derived functors continue right-exact ones to the left (Tor from ⊗), right-derived continue left-exact ones to the right (Ext from Hom). They measure exactly what the original functor destroys.

examples.explanation: Tor appears where tensoring breaks exactness on the left.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Chain complex
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

notes: Tor/Ext lecture structure cross-checked against UT Austin homological-algebra lecture-note excerpts (Lecture 5).

name: Tor and Ext
definition: The derived functors of tensor product (Tor, left-derived) and Hom (Ext, right-derived). Tor₁ detects torsion killed by tensoring; Ext¹ classifies extensions 0 → B → ? → A → 0 up to equivalence.

examples.explanation: With d = gcd(m, n): tensoring detects exactly the shared torsion.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Chain complex
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

notes: Standard formulas cross-checked against UT Austin homological-algebra lecture-note excerpts (Lecture 5: derived functors, Tor and Ext).

name: Chain homotopy
definition: Chain maps differing by dh + hd for degree-shifting maps h: homotopic in the algebraic sense. Homotopic maps induce the identical map on homology, the algebraic shadow of homotopic spaces giving equal homology.

examples.explanation: The difference factors through the differentials, hence vanishes on homology classes.

sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Affine variety
definition: The common zero locus V(S) of polynomials in affine space, an affine algebraic set, and a variety when irreducible (not a union of two proper closed subsets). Equations become geometry.

examples.explanation: The parabola as a plane curve: an irreducible affine variety.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Algebraic variety
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Projective variety
definition: Zero loci of homogeneous polynomials in projective space, where scaling doesn't matter. Projective space adds points at infinity, making varieties complete (compact-like): parallel lines finally meet.

examples.explanation: The projective line: an affine line plus one point at infinity, topologically a circle.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Algebraic variety
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Coordinate ring
definition: Polynomial functions on V: the polynomial ring modulo the ideal of functions vanishing on V. Hilbert's Nullstellensatz makes this the algebra-geometry dictionary, points match maximal ideals, irreducible means integral domain.

examples.explanation: Functions on the parabola: polynomials identified wherever they agree on it.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Algebraic variety
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Zariski topology
definition: The topology whose closed sets are exactly the algebraic sets. Far coarser than Euclidean: on an irreducible variety every nonempty open is dense, and on the affine line the closed sets are just finite sets plus everything.

examples.explanation: Closed subsets of the affine line: finite point sets and the whole line, nothing in between.

commonMistakes: Expecting Hausdorff separation; distinct points need not have disjoint Zariski neighborhoods.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Algebraic variety
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Regular and rational functions
definition: Regular functions are locally polynomial (ratios with nonvanishing denominator); rational functions are defined on some dense open, forming the function field. Morphisms of varieties are maps given locally by regular functions.

examples.explanation: Regular on A¹ minus the origin, rational on all of A¹: defined almost everywhere.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Algebraic variety
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Dimension of a variety
definition: The length of the longest chain of irreducible closed subsets (Krull dimension): curves have 1, surfaces 2. Equivalently the transcendence degree of the function field, the number of independent parameters.

examples.explanation: Plane ⊃ curve ⊃ point: a chain of length two, matching two coordinates.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Algebraic variety
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Singular and nonsingular points
definition: Points where a variety fails to be manifold-like, detected by the Jacobian criterion: all defining partials vanish. A node has distinct tangents, a cusp has coincident ones; elsewhere the (Zariski) tangent space has the expected dimension.

examples.explanation: Cusp at the origin: both partials vanish there, so no well-defined tangent.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Algebraic variety
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Scheme
definition: A locally ringed space locally isomorphic to spectra of rings: varieties generalized to allow nilpotents (x² = 0 thickens the origin infinitesimally) and non-closed points. Spec R has prime ideals as points; a variety over k is a separated finite-type integral scheme.

examples.explanation: One generic point plus a closed point per prime: arithmetic as geometry.

commonMistakes: Treating schemes as varieties with fancier words; nilpotents and generic points are genuinely new content.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Algebraic variety
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Sheaf (and stalk)
definition: Local data attached to opens with restriction maps, satisfying locality (matching restrictions agree) and gluing (compatible local data assemble uniquely). The stalk at a point is the germ-level limit, the local ring in scheme theory.

examples.explanation: Continuous (or regular, or smooth) functions on each open U: restricting and gluing work as expected.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Sheaf (mathematics)
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Local ring
definition: A ring with exactly one maximal ideal: everything outside it is a unit. Stalks of structure sheaves and localizations (e.g. rationals with odd denominator) are the archetypes, algebra zoomed into one point.

examples.explanation: Integers localized away from 2: the unique maximal ideal is the even numerators.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Algebraic variety
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Group representation
definition: A homomorphism from a group into automorphisms of a vector space: each group element acts as an invertible linear map, turning abstract symmetry into matrices. The space acted on is the representation space; injective means faithful.
reading: “rho from G to G L of V”.

examples.explanation: Rotations of the plane: angles add because matrices multiply.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Group representation
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Invariant subspaces and subrepresentations
definition: A subspace carried into itself by every group element: ρ(g)W ⊆ W for all g. Restricting the action gives a subrepresentation, a smaller representation living inside.

examples.explanation: Rotation about the z-axis fixes that axis: a one-dimensional subrepresentation.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Group representation
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Irreducible representation
definition: A nonzero representation with no proper subrepresentations: the atoms of the theory. Complete reducibility (splitting into irreducibles) needs hypotheses, Maschke's theorem gives it when the characteristic avoids the group order, e.g. always over ℂ for finite groups.

examples.explanation: Plane rotations: no real line stays put, so this two-dimensional representation is irreducible over ℝ.

commonMistakes: Assuming every representation splits; modular representations (characteristic dividing |G|) need not be completely reducible.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Group representation
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Character of a representation
definition: The trace function χ(g) = tr(ρ(g)): a class function constant on conjugacy classes. Over ℂ, the character determines a finite-group representation up to isomorphism, and irreducible characters are orthonormal.

examples.explanation: Trace of the rotation matrix: the character sees the angle, not the basis.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Group representation
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Schur's lemma
definition: A nonzero equivariant map between irreducibles is an isomorphism, there is nothing in between. Consequently, over an algebraically closed field, equivariant self-maps are just scalars.

examples.explanation: Any G-linear endomorphism of a complex irreducible is a scalar matrix.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Schur's lemma
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Group algebra
definition: Formal linear combinations of group elements with convolution product extending the group law. Representations of G are exactly modules over ℂ[G]; its dimension is |G| for finite groups.

examples.explanation: Basis indexed by group elements for finite G.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Group representation
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Induced and restricted representations
definition: Restriction views a representation through a subgroup; induction builds a G-representation from an H-representation on cosets (Frobenius reciprocity relates their Hom-spaces). Inducing the trivial rep gives permutation action on cosets.

examples.explanation: Inducing the trivial representation: G permuting the cosets of H.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Group representation
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Lie algebra representation
definition: A Lie algebra homomorphism into matrices, preserving brackets: the infinitesimal version of a Lie group representation, obtained by differentiating at the identity. For semisimple algebras, irreducibles are classified by highest weights.

examples.explanation: Pauli matrices: the spin-1/2 representation, with bracket relations matching su(2).

sources.label: Wikipedia, Group representation
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Smooth manifold
definition: A Hausdorff, second-countable topological space with a maximal smooth atlas: locally Euclidean with smooth transitions, so calculus works globally. The Hausdorff and countability hypotheses buy bump functions and partitions of unity.

examples.explanation: The circle with its standard smooth structure: locally an interval, globally a loop.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Differentiable manifold
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Charts and atlases
definition: A chart identifies an open patch with Euclidean space; an atlas covers the manifold. It is smooth when all transition maps between overlapping charts are smooth, the maximal such atlas is the smooth structure itself.

examples.explanation: The transition map: re-expressing one chart's coordinates in another's, required smooth.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Differentiable manifold
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Tangent space
definition: The n-dimensional vector space of directions at p: derivations on germs (or velocity vectors of curves, or chart-based vectors, equivalent views). Not the calculus tangent line: that is one affine line, this is the whole linear space of directions.

examples.explanation: The line touching the circle at p: every direction of travel through p.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Differentiable manifold
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Vector field
definition: A smooth choice of tangent vector at every point: a section of the tangent bundle. Integral curves follow the arrows; their collective motion is the flow.

examples.explanation: Counterclockwise rotation field: integral curves are concentric circles.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Differentiable manifold
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Differential form
definition: Alternating multilinear machines eating tangent vectors and returning numbers: the natural integrands on manifolds. The wedge product combines them; pullback transports them along smooth maps.

examples.explanation: The area form: feeding two vectors returns their signed spanned area.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Differentiable manifold
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Riemannian metric
definition: A smoothly varying inner product on each tangent space: it defines lengths, angles, and volumes. There is then a unique torsion-free compatible connection (Levi-Civita) doing the differentiating.

examples.explanation: The flat Euclidean metric: Pythagoras infinitesimally.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Differentiable manifold
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Geodesic
definition: Locally length-minimizing constant-speed curves: autoparallel transport of their own velocity (∇_γ̇γ̇ = 0). Great circles on spheres; straight lines in flat space.

examples.explanation: Equators and meridians: the shortest routes on a sphere.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Differentiable manifold
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Connection and covariant derivative
definition: Differentiates vector fields along directions with the Leibniz rule: ∇_X Y. Christoffel symbols are its coordinates; metric-compatible and torsion-free gives the unique Levi-Civita connection. Shares its glyph with the gradient, a different concept.

examples.explanation: The covariant derivative of Y in direction X: ordinary directional derivative plus correction terms.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Differentiable manifold
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Curvature (and torsion)
definition: Measures path-dependence of parallel transport: second covariant derivatives fail to commute by the Riemann tensor. Zero means flat; sectional and Gaussian curvatures are its two-dimensional faces. Torsion separately measures frame-twisting.

examples.explanation: On a positively curved sphere, triangle angles sum past 180°.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Differentiable manifold
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Exterior derivative
definition: Sends k-forms to (k+1)-forms with d² = 0, unifying gradient, curl, and divergence. Closed forms (dω = 0) modulo exact ones (ω = dη) is de Rham cohomology.

examples.explanation: On functions it is the total differential: gradient in form language.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Differentiable manifold
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Stokes' theorem
definition: ∫_M dω = ∫_{∂M} ω: integrating a derivative over a region equals integrating the form over its boundary. One statement unifying the fundamental theorem of calculus, Green, classical Stokes, and Gauss.

examples.explanation: The one-dimensional case: boundary of [a, b] is its two endpoints.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Differentiable manifold
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Tensor fields
definition: Smoothly varying multilinear maps on tangent and cotangent spaces, of type (r, s). The metric and curvature are examples. A bare array of numbers is not a tensor: the transformation law under change of coordinates is the content.

examples.explanation: The metric as a (0,2)-tensor: it eats two vectors and returns their inner product.

commonMistakes: Calling any multi-indexed array a tensor; without the transformation law it is just numbers in boxes.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Differentiable manifold
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Pushforward and pullback
definition: A smooth map F: M → N pushes tangent vectors forward (dF, the Jacobian in coordinates) and pulls functions and forms back (F*). Vectors go with the map; covectors and forms go against it.

examples.explanation: The best linear approximation of F at p, sending directions to directions.

sources.label: Wikipedia, Differentiable manifold
sources.license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Lie derivative
definition: Differentiates tensors by dragging them along a vector field's flow, no connection or metric needed. Cartan's formula L_X = dι_X + ι_Xd ties it to the exterior derivative; on functions it is just the directional derivative.

examples.explanation: On functions: differentiate f in the X direction.
